system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You were admitted to the hospital on 11/08/2020 and discharged on 01/02/2021, staying for 1 month, 24 days, and 15 hours. You came in with severe pain in your lower left back that started three days before, along with weakness (asthenia) and difficulty walking (altered gait). The person with you said you did not have fever, nausea, or vomiting. There was some discharge from the dressing of your catheter (a tube placed in your body) in your right thigh vein (femoral vein).

During your hospital stay, it was found that you had a bloodstream infection (infection in your blood) caused by a bacteria called Staphylococcus aureus MRSA. This infection led to several other problems:
1.  A bloodstream infection linked to the Schilley catheter (a type of tube) in your right thigh vein.
2.  Bacterial endocarditis (an infection of the inner lining of your heart), specifically affecting your mitral valve (one of the heart valves). An echocardiogram (a heart ultrasound) on 11/18 showed a "vegetation" (a growth caused by infection) on this valve.
3.  Pyogenic spondylodiscitis (an infection of the spinal bones and the discs between them) in your L3/L4 area (lower back). On 11/05, you had low back pain and difficulty walking. A CT scan (a special X-ray) of your lower back on 11/12 showed signs of a possible fracture (break) in your L1 spinal bone due to weak bones, and gas in your spinal canal at L2/L3, which might be from a slipped disc. An infection or inflammation could not be ruled out. A lumbar MRI (a detailed scan of your lower back) on 25/11/2020 confirmed infectious spondylodiscitis with an anterior epidural abscess (a collection of pus in front of your spinal cord).
4.  A left ileopsoas abscess (a collection of pus in a muscle in your abdomen/hip area). An MRI on 25/10/2020 showed a collection of pus in your left ileopsoas muscle, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm, with swelling (edema) around it.

The catheter was removed on 11/08, and you were started on antibiotic medicine called Vancomycin, based on culture reports (tests to identify bacteria). An attempt was made on 12/02 by the {organization} to drain the pus from the psoas abscess using a needle (percutaneous drainage), but it could not be done because your intestines were in the way.

You showed improvement in the infection in your spine (axial lesions) with the treatment, and the doctors continued with medicines to treat the infections found during your stay. You did not have a fever, and your blood cultures (tests for infection in blood) repeatedly came back negative.

Because you were not moving much, you developed a sacral pressure injury (a bedsore on your lower back). This was treated with surgical debridement (cleaning the wound by removing dead tissue) and other local treatments. The team gave you instructions on how to care for this injury at home.

You also needed hemodialysis (a machine that filters your blood when your kidneys don't work well) on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. This was done through an arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein) in your left arm, but there was some narrowing (stenosis) in it. You are currently on this kidney treatment.

When you were discharged, your general condition was good. You were a bit pale, hydrated (had enough fluids), not blue (acyanotic), not jaundiced (anicteric), did not have a fever, and were breathing normally (eupneic) in room air.
Neurology: You were conscious and knew the time, place, and who you were.
Respiratory: Your lungs sounded clear on both sides, with some minor crackling sounds at the bottom, but no signs of breathing difficulty.
Cardiac: Your heart rhythm was irregular, but the heart sounds were normal, with no murmurs (extra heart sounds).
Abdomen: Your stomach was a bit swollen, bowel sounds were present, it was not tense, and not painful when touched lightly or deeply. There were no signs of irritation in the lining of your abdomen.
Your hands and feet were warm and had good blood flow.
Upper limbs: The fistula in your left arm had a good "thrill" (a vibration felt over the fistula, indicating it's working).
Lower limbs: You had some mild swelling (edema) and reddish-brown skin discoloration (ochre dermatitis) on your shins.

Cultures (tests for bacteria) showed:
*   Catheter tip on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus, sensitive to Vancomycin.
*   Blood culture on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus.
*   Blood culture on 11/11: Staphylococcus aureus, resistant to Oxacillin (oxa r) in two samples.
*   Blood culture on 11/21: Citrobacter koseri in one sample, Staphylococcus aureus in one sample.
*   Blood culture on 11/24: Staphylococcus capitis.
*   Blood cultures on 11/28, 12/01, and 12/02 were negative.

An MRI of your pelvis was done on 12/16. It was arranged with [organization] for you to attend hemodialysis at [organization] on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, with transport by stretcher taxi from your city.

You are being discharged with the following instructions and pending issues:
*   You need to take 0.5 grams of Vancomycin (an antibiotic) after each scheduled hemodialysis session. This antibiotic treatment will continue until 01/09/2021, completing 6 weeks after your last negative blood culture.
*   Your arteriovenous fistula needs to be checked. A phlebography (a special X-ray of veins) of the fistula is recommended to find the site of narrowing (stenosis). This will help decide if another phlebography or an ultrasound before the procedure is needed. You have been put on a list for this. [organization] will contact you to schedule this treatment.
*   For your sacral pressure injury, the specialist team noted that your follow-up appointment is on 16/01/2021 for reassessment. You were given instructions for home care of the injury.
*   You need cardiology (heart doctor) follow-up to investigate amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal protein builds up in organs). You missed an appointment on 09/09, and a new one is scheduled for 01/13 for motor rehabilitation (physical therapy). We are waiting for an appointment from the physiatry department (physical medicine and rehabilitation) at [organization], which was requested on 12/27.
*   The nuclear magnetic resonance (MRI) report of your pelvis from 12/16 needs to be checked.
*   Your previous long-term medications will be continued.
*   You will go for dialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays.
*   Your cardiology outpatient clinic appointment for amyloidosis is on 01/13.
*   Your pressure injury surgery outpatient clinic appointment is on 01/16.
